terms.def: The seller: an online shop or business that sends parcels through Carrybee. Uses the aladdin panel.
One shop owned by a merchant. One login can own several businesses; each has its own stores, price plan, invoices and payout account.
A large business account created by Carrybee staff rather than by self-signup, usually with special pricing.
A staff member the merchant adds to their business, with role operator (handles orders) or accountant (handles money).
The buyer who receives the parcel and pays the COD amount.
The Carrybee rider who picks up and delivers parcels. Always called agent in code. Uses a separate mobile app that is not in these repos.
Agent productivity split: riders delivering inside their own city vs riders working outside it.
How a rider is paid: a fixed salary or a commission per parcel. Paid into their salary wallet (bank or MFS).
Key Account Manager. Looks after large merchants: pricing, pickups, receivable invoices. kam_lead manages KAMs.
Runs one hub: assigns runs, closes runs, counts cash and submits the hub deposit.
Managers over a group of hubs (cluster) or a group of clusters (region). They approve claims in reconciliation.
Head of operations. First approver for petty cash and rent.
Finance roles late in the approval chain: audit checks a claim, accounts releases the money.
Staff who approve or reject riders' urgent approval requests and look for fake requests.
Highest access level. Can use G-Mode repair tools and impersonate other users.
Owner of a building Carrybee rents for a hub. Rent is paid through petty cash.
A Carrybee branch where parcels are received, sorted and sent out. Called warehouse in some menus and code paths.
The hub near the seller where a parcel first enters the network.
The hub near the buyer that delivers the parcel.
Where the parcel physically is right now.
A hub that also sorts parcels coming from other hubs before sending them on.
The main sorting centre (hub IDs 71 and 72 in code). Most long-distance parcels pass through it.
A regional sorting centre between the central warehouse and the last-mile hubs.
The organisation tree. A region contains clusters, a cluster contains hubs. Each level has a lead.
The address tree used for delivery. A zone belongs to a hub; areas and sectors are smaller parts of it.
A hub's set of zones that one rider covers, with a default agent. Types: pickup, delivery, reverse pickup.
A fixed trunk route between hubs that baskets travel along, with a base code and sub codes.
Inside Dhaka, Outside Dhaka and sub area: the three delivery zones that set price, COD fee and return fee. The code labels spell these out.
Size class of a hub: big, mid or small.
The map boundary of a delivery zone, drawn in the geonix tool.
When creating a basket, the destination can be another LMH or the hub's own (self) team.
A merchant's pickup or return address, linked to a hub and route. One is the default pickup store and one the default return store.
A new store waiting for ops approval and for its map location to be verified.
Used almost interchangeably: one shipment from a merchant to a buyer. Consignment is the formal word used in IDs and reports.
Carrybee's unique ID for one parcel, printed on the label and used for tracking.
The seller's own order number, kept alongside the consignment ID.
Cash the rider must collect from the buyer. Zero for prepaid orders.
The item's actual value, used for compensation if lost or damaged.
Parcel weight in kg. Weight above the base slab costs extra per kg.
A category for the goods inside. Used by the legal panel to filter orders. The allowed values are not visible in the frontend.
Regular or express delivery. Express is faster and costs more.
How the order was created: single form, bulk sheet, OCR from a photo, developer API, or by ops staff.
Creating many orders at once from a spreadsheet.
Create an order by uploading a photo; the buyer's name, phone and address are read from it automatically.
Deliver a new item and take the old one back in the same visit. Costs an exchange fee.
A rider collects an item from the buyer and returns it to the seller, without a new delivery.
A normal pickup from the seller's store, as opposed to a reverse pickup from the buyer.
Redirect a failed or returned parcel to a different buyer instead of returning it.
The merchant asks Carrybee to collect N parcels from a store. Pickup time is about 4–7 pm.
In this codebase POD means the printed parcel label with barcode and QR code. POS POD is the small thermal-printer version.
Whether the POD label has been printed for an order yet.
Free-text instructions from the seller for the rider.

A flag the seller ticks when creating an order: the parcel must stay sealed and the buyer may not open it to check the item before paying. Shown as a box icon in the order list and printed as CLOSE BOX on the label. Off by default; in a bulk sheet the column is 1 or 0.
While a parcel is moving, the seller can ask Carrybee to hold it or to deliver it urgently.
The numeric status of a parcel (1–45, 53). Every scan or action moves it to a new number. The merchant panel shows a simpler text version.
Order created, not yet requested for pickup.
Seller asked for a pickup.
A rider is assigned to collect it.
Rider has the parcel.
Pickup paused or cancelled. A cancelled pickup can be reopened.
Parcel arrived at the first-mile hub.
On the way to, then at, a sorting hub.
On the way to, then at, the central warehouse.
On the way to, then received at, the hub that will deliver it.
In a rider's delivery run.
Buyer received the parcel and paid. A final status.
Delivery paused, for example the buyer asked for another day. It will be attempted again.
Delivery failed and the parcel will go back to the seller.
Buyer kept only part of the order; the rest is returned.
Parcel was damaged while with Carrybee. Compensation may apply.
Parcel cannot be found. Compensation is paid and charged to the agent, hub or Carrybee.
A return where the buyer still paid the delivery charge.
Exchange completed: new item delivered, old item collected.
A return travelling back: pending at hub → sorting hub → central → first-mile hub → on the way to merchant.
The seller has the returned parcel back. A final status.
A returned parcel kept in Carrybee's inventory instead of being handed to the seller.
Moving between hubs on a transfer run.
A parcel marked lost has turned up again.
Put a returned or problem parcel back into the delivery flow. Sellers can reprocess returns until 7 am.
On the way to, or at, a sub-sort centre, for deliveries (38, 39) or returns (40, 41).
A reverse pickup: waiting, assigned, picked, or on hold.
The buyer or seller asked to change the order (for example address or recipient).
A status where the parcel's journey ends: delivered, returned to merchant, lost, damaged and similar. Changing it needs G-Mode.
The merchant panel groups statuses into tabs: active, delivered, returning, returned.
One trip by an agent, with a list of parcels. Status: pending → started → transferring → closed.
A trip to collect parcels from merchants' stores.
A trip to deliver parcels to buyers. The agent app sends delivery start and end events.
Moves baskets between hubs along a linehaul.
Hands returned parcels back to merchants.
Collects items from buyers (reverse pickups).
Attach baskets, stores or parcels to a specific agent's run.
Add or remove parcels from a run or basket by scanning their barcode.
One hub hands a transfer run over; the next receives it by scanning, in bulk or one by one.
Printed paperwork that travels with a run, listing what it carries.
A code stored on every run. Probably the seal or lock code for the vehicle or basket.
Ending a run. For delivery runs, the cash is counted at this point.
Manager closes a delivery run with remarks when the agent app never sent its delivery-end event.
Runs left open, meaning their cash is not yet accounted for.
Move a parcel to another zone or another hub when it was routed to the wrong place.
Move a parcel from one agent's run to another's.
One try at delivering a parcel. Extra attempts beyond the included one can be charged.

terms.t: First mile / middle mile / last mile
terms.def: The three legs of the trip: store to first hub, hub to hub, and last hub to the buyer's door.
Whether a parcel at the hub has been checked in and grouped by destination yet, for deliveries and for returns.
First-mile hub check-in: weigh, sort or unsort, view the consignment log.
A sealed bag of parcels moved between hubs as one unit. Status: created → printed → assigned → reached → opened → received.
At the central warehouse: scan parcels, correct their last-mile hub, pack outgoing baskets.
Sorting racks with 12 or 24 pigeon holes, each mapped to a hub or linehaul. Short for Point to Network.
One slot in a PTN rack. Parcels for the same destination go in the same hole.
Every scan and status change for one parcel, with time and hub.
The seller brings parcels to the hub. Confirmed by an OTP sent to the seller.
A rider asks to change an outcome (return, price change, exchange, partial delivery, paid return). The seller or QC must approve it.
The buyer pays a different amount than the order said. Needs approval.
The merchant's queue of things needing action: urgent approvals, partial deliveries, returns, no-entry parcels, last-mile issues.
Problems at the final delivery: buyer unreachable, wrong address, repeated failed attempts.
A parcel physically at a hub with no matching order in the system. Ops create the order, process it or return it.
An order missing data needed to move it on, such as zone or weight.
When a basket is scanned in: a parcel that should be there but isn't (missing), or one that shouldn't be (extra).
Reasons for a zone or hub transfer: sorted to the wrong route, sent by the previous hub to the wrong place, or the address is on a border.
Money paid to the seller for a lost or damaged parcel. Charged to the agent, hub or Carrybee.
A seller reports a buyer for COD refusal (won't pay) or return abuse. Ops approve or reject it. The fraud checker shows a phone number's history.
An urgent approval a rider raised without a real reason, tracked by hub and agent.
How long parcels have been sitting at a stage. Old parcels signal a backlog.
A merchant's rate card: delivery fee by zone and weight, COD fee, return fee and extra charges.
Price bands by destination (ISD, OSD, sub area) and weight. Each extra kg above the base costs more.
Carrybee's charge for delivering one parcel.
Carrybee's charge for collecting cash, usually a percentage of the amount (1% shown in the UI). Different for ISD, OSD and sub area.
Charge for returning a failed parcel, as a percentage of the delivery fee.
Extra services on top of delivery: packaging, extra delivery attempts, reverse pickup.
A lower price for a merchant. KAMs request it; it needs approval.
Delivery fee + COD fee + extra charges − discount for one order.
Business account types. Postpaid accounts are billed later and can owe Carrybee; prepaid pay up front.
Whether a business may send cash-on-delivery orders.
How much a business may owe Carrybee before it must pay. The exact effect (blocking orders or not) isn't visible in the frontend.
Cash on delivery: the buyer pays the rider in cash. Carrybee keeps its fees and passes the rest to the seller.
Cash actually collected from the buyer. Can differ from the amount to collect (partial delivery, price change).

aka: COD expected but not yet collected
terms.def: Cash Carrybee expects to collect on parcels still in progress.
Amounts also stored in paisa (1/100 of a taka) to avoid rounding errors. Spelled paisha in code.
Count of each banknote (1000, 500, 200, 100, 50…) the agent hands in when a delivery run closes.
Cash a hub keeps instead of depositing. Subtracted from the hub's deposit.
Cash carried forward from a previous period and added to what the hub must deposit.
Collected cash that went missing. Subtracted from the hub's deposit and tracked separately.
A hub's deposit of collected cash. Payable = sum collected − (money lost + cash in hand + withdrawn expenses) + carry.
The cash book for each hub: cash in hand and carry over time.
A delivered order whose COD is ready to be deposited or paid to the seller.
Payable: Carrybee owes the seller (COD exceeds fees). Receivable: the seller owes Carrybee (fees exceed COD).
A statement for a business: COD collected minus fees plus compensation = amount paid out. Status: unpaid → processing → paid.
Two ways to generate payout invoices. Positive invoices cover accounts with a positive balance, where Carrybee owes the seller.
A one-off invoice outside the normal cycle.
An invoice being paid: exported to the bank as an Excel file and processed in bulk.
Real-Time Gross Settlement, Bangladesh Bank's same-day system for large transfers. Big payouts are tagged RTGS.
How often a seller is paid: regular cycle, custom schedule, or on demand.
A seller asks to be paid now for chosen consignments instead of waiting for the cycle.
Where the seller is paid: a bank account (with branch) or an MFS wallet.
Mobile Financial Service: mobile wallets like bKash and Nagad.
A seller's new or changed payout account, waiting for finance approval.
Money a seller owes Carrybee. Postpaid accounts get a monthly invoice.
The seller pays what they owe through bKash, Nagad, SSLCommerz or bank transfer.
Accounting view of invoices: when Carrybee's fee income is booked. Permission name in the accounts app.
Order and fee export for the legal team, filtered by parcel type.
Small hub expenses. Approved through ops head → HR → audit → accounts, then withdrawn with an OTP.
Monthly hub rent paid to landlords, approved like petty cash.
Expenses the hub has already taken out of collected cash. Subtracted from the hub deposit.
Approved petty cash or allowance is released only after the receiver confirms an OTP.
Pay to agents based on runs and distance, released by OTP.
Checking and approving allowance and expense claims, sometimes adjusting the distance. Chain: cluster lead → region lead → HR → audit → accounts.
The ordered list of people who must approve a claim. Each 'Waiting for…' status names the next approver.
One-time password by SMS. Used for login, signup, hub drop-off, cash withdrawals, and delivery confirmation.
Single sign-on: hive staff log in through a central login.
Support staff log in as another user to see and fix their problem.
Restricted repair area: reopen runs, reset OTPs or agent throttling, change final statuses, regenerate invoices, bulk cancel.
A block on an agent's login after too many attempts; G-Mode can reset it.
Access keys like merchant.parcel.add that decide which pages and buttons a user sees.
Electronic identity check of a merchant using their national ID card (NID) or birth certificate.
Lets a seller's own website create orders through an API and receive status updates via webhooks.
Real-time messaging server used for live chat between sellers and riders.
Push notification service. Sellers get alerts for returns, urgent approvals, invoices, with do-not-disturb.
Referral QR codes and short links to sign up new merchants, with visit counts.
Map service for zone boundaries. Dry run previews a change before saving it.
Share of parcels delivered. Also shown per buyer phone number in the fraud checker.
Share of parcels returned or put on hold. High values point to bad buyers, addresses or riders.
The time window a day's numbers count. The sorting window runs from 18:00 to 06:00 the next day.
Parcels still in progress at a hub, broken down by attempt and age.
How many runs were closed and how many parcels each agent handled.
Average score buyers and sellers give an agent.
A merchant who stopped sending parcels.
CSV export of orders with their fees, statuses and hubs.
